[[cobalt-release-measurements]]
== Release measurements of the shipped implementation

These local measurements compare Boost-backed native interfaces with the shipped Wasm implementation on one machine. They are not a cross-machine performance guarantee. See the raw environment, commands, hashes and samples accompanying the tables.

Sizes cover `-O2`, `-O3`, `-Os` and `-Oz`, each with full LTO off/on. Runtime comparisons use `-O3` without LTO across every feasible profile. All builds use Release and `NDEBUG`. EH-on uses `-fwasm-exceptions` for JSPI/WASI and `-fexceptions` for Asyncify in this toolchain. Those comparisons include the selected exception code generation, not suspension alone. The workload executable contains seven finite matched workloads, not an unchanged upstream application. The baseline contains only an empty runner. Browser payload is JavaScript plus Wasm; native is a Mach-O executable. Runtime installations and native system shared libraries are outside these payload sizes.

All 136 optimization/profile builds also execute the empty runner and seven short checked workloads for both libraries: 2,176 payload qualification runs in native, Node or Wasmtime. They validate the size artifacts; their timings are excluded from the performance tables. Real-browser measurements and correctness observations below remain separate.

Single/multi are B2 threading properties. Native single does not disable Boost threads; Wasm multi selects the thread-capable SDK profile. Each workload runs one context on one execution thread. This is not a multicore throughput comparison. P3 threads are cooperative.

Build time is one forced rebuild of six programs per setting with three compiler jobs and a warmed SDK cache. No other build/test from this session ran concurrently; other user and OS activity is not controlled. A single build is an observation, not a timing distribution.

=== Interpreting the native comparison

Every workload constructs a channel and timer before its loop, including the post-only loop. The initialized reactor remains part of that context. On this macOS/Boost combination, the native scheduler polls kqueue between posted completions. Therefore the ratios compare these initialized-reactor applications, not the intrinsic cost of an isolated coroutine or post. They must not be generalized to Linux, Windows, or a context that never initializes I/O. The native Cobalt runner also registers POSIX signals, unlike its WASI runner.

A separate diagnostic uses unmodified Boost and changes only whether it constructs an idle timer before 10,000 checked posts. Five pairs observed 59.5-98.9 ns/post without that timer and 10.50-12.15 us/post with it. This supports the initialized-reactor explanation for the large native post/channel ratios. It is a boundary check with fixed order and no discarded warmup, not a replacement statistical benchmark. Its source, command and output are retained as `native-reactor-control` files beside the results; the immutable source snapshot is `.cpp.txt`. Copy it to the recorded `.cpp` path before replaying that historical command. The main samples are unchanged.

=== Versioned toolchain diagnostics

8 WASIp3 LTO build configurations report the SDK 34 linker diagnostic `function signature mismatch: cabi_realloc`. A minimal malloc/printf program using only the SDK reproduces it and runs successfully in Wasmtime. The warning is preserved in build receipts; all measured payloads also pass their separate short execution checks. This does not establish that every canonical-ABI path is safe with this SDK/LTO combination. The primary runtime comparison uses no LTO. Native no-EH Cobalt retains its upstream promise diagnostic and issue-287 warning; neither warning is hidden or treated as proof that the affected move path is safe.

=== Runtime and memory scope

Each operation is one completed iteration: `post` resumes once; `immediate` sends then receives in a buffered Asio channel; `channel` transfers one value through an unbuffered channel; `parallel` joins one Asio-channel send/receive pair; `allocation` performs five posts and five arena allocations; `timer` awaits a zero-expiry timer; `http` parses one complete in-memory HTTP response. Asio uses `parallel_group` and Cobalt uses `join` for paired operations. HTTP does not measure network or TLS latency. Every iteration contributes to a checked checksum.

Thirty fresh executions per workload/profile use frozen common operation counts and an in-process warmup. The report records median, p95, min/max and a bootstrap 95% interval for the median. Ten baseline starts measure fresh process/page startup. The browser process is retained; each page/worker is new, with no-store HTTP. OS and engine caches are not cleared, so these are not cold-machine or empty-code-cache measurements. The explicit buffered loader measures fetch, compile and instantiate separately; it does not represent the default streaming loader.

Three instrumented executions describe {cpp} allocation counts/requested bytes and Cobalt frame PMR requests. Those nested counters must not be added. Direct C malloc and JavaScript allocations are outside their scope. Wasm linear memory is capacity, not live heap. Process RSS includes Node/Wasmtime; browser-module RSS/CPU are unavailable. Instrumentation timing is retained only as a diagnostic, not a comparative performance claim.

=== Baseline startup and instrumented allocation workload

Startup is the median of ten fresh starts. Process wall time includes harness setup, runtime launch and waiting; browser wall time begins inside a fresh page/worker, after its host page navigation, and includes buffered module loading. They are different observation boundaries. `n/a` means unavailable, not zero. Memory columns below use three instrumented allocation-workload runs. Complete workload-specific memory distributions and separate JS/Wasm/native payload bytes are in the CSV files.

=== Complete evidence and plots

`bench/results/2026-11-07` contains `sizes.csv`, `metrics.csv`, `summary.json`, environment metadata and the raw evidence archive with its SHA-256 file. The archive retains commands, build logs, source/artifact hashes, calibration, frozen counts and every independent sample. The local experiment is not remote CI evidence.
